intro: Three items this week, all sourced from Product Hunt. Not a curation choice: HN and GitHub genuinely turned up nothing that cleared the fintech/compliance bar in today's pull, which says more about a single day's sample than about either site. The three that did clear it share something worth noticing anyway — each puts the AI agent behind a constraint it doesn't get a vote on: a static analyzer that isn't AI, an architecture that keeps credentials off someone else's cloud, a compliance layer built into OT/ICS instead of bolted on after. Nobody here is selling "just trust the model." We'll take it.

items.title: Mustel
items.note: Mustel wires Bandit (security) and pip-audit (dependency vulnerabilities) directly into the agent loop for Cursor, Claude Code, and Windsurf, compressing findings into a prompt an agent can act on instead of surfacing raw linter noise. The framing is worth noting on its own: it bills itself as "non-AI" static analysis feeding an AI agent — a deterministic, auditable check sitting in front of a coding agent's output, not another agent wrapper. A separate Audit Mode runs deeper checks in CI, distinct from the fast local dev-mode scan.

items.title: QuantDinger
items.note: QuantDinger is a self-hosted, open-source quant trading OS that connects Cursor, Claude Code, or Codex through 25 scoped MCP tools — with strategies, credentials, and trading data explicitly kept on the user's own infrastructure rather than a vendor's cloud. For a fintech engineering team that can't send trading credentials or proprietary strategy logic to a third-party API, that's the adoption question answered by architecture rather than by a compliance add-on bolted onto a SaaS product. It also markets producing "auditable" Python strategies from LLM-assisted research — worth watching for how that claim gets substantiated as the project matures, since the excerpt doesn't say what makes a generated strategy auditable beyond being readable Python.

items.title: Basalt
items.note: Basalt generates architecture diagrams from a plain-English stack description, and explicitly extends into OT/ICS (operational technology/industrial control systems) with what it describes as compliance checks built into that layer — a category most architecture-diagramming tools stop short of. For engineers documenting infrastructure spanning cloud and industrial/OT environments, a tool treating OT/ICS as first-class rather than an afterthought is worth a look. The excerpt doesn't say which compliance frameworks those built-in checks actually cover, which is the first question to ask before relying on them.
